Carleton has earned the Carnegie Elective Classification for Sustainability, becoming one of the first 14 institutions nationally to receive this new recognition. The new classification, developed by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching and the American Council on Education (ACE), recognizes institutions that successfully integrate sustainability across areas including curriculum, research, operations, career preparation, and community engagement. Each of the 14 institutions will be part of the inaugural cohort of classified institutions, which will be announced in June 2027 alongside the institutions participating in the first full classification cycle. 

In 2025, Carleton was one of 20 institutions that participated in the pilot program, collaborating with a diverse set of colleges and universities in a national community of practice to test and help shape the classification’s framework and application process. As part of the program, the College completed a collaborative and rigorous self-study and provided feedback on the Carnegie framework, prompts, evidence requirements, and review process. Through this process, many offices and partners worked together to document the breadth of sustainability work happening at Carleton, including the Sustainability Office, CCCE, the Grants Office, Facilities, Career Center, Cowling Arboretum, Bon Appétit, and the City of Northfield. 

“Uncovering strategies and examples used across the College helps to not only tell our story, but to make connections shaping our work,” said Sarah Fortner, director of sustainability at Carleton. “In addition, the future research done across the institutions that receive the elective will inform how we support and make progress in higher education sustainability.”

This achievement is a reflection of the longstanding work of faculty, staff, and students to advance sustainability and environmental justice through education, community engagement, and operations. Particular areas of work that stood out in Carleton’s review include the Cowling Arboretum as a laboratory for research and classroom learning, support for student climate leadership through the Sustainable Futures Framework, and the College’s strong history of decarbonization both on-campus and through local collaboration. 

The Carnegie Elective Classification for Sustainability is hosted by the University of Colorado Boulder, working alongside the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching and the American Council on Education. All institutions who receive the classification will retain it for six years, through 2033.

“The first group of inaugural institutions help bring this new classification to life,” said Timothy F.C. Knowles, president of the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching. “We’re proud to recognize their leadership and the many ways they are advancing sustainability across their campuses and communities.”

The Sustainability Elective Classification is one of a distinguished suite of Carnegie Elective Classifications, including Community Engagement and Leadership for Public Purpose. This initiative highlights higher education’s transformative role in addressing societal challenges and creating sustainable futures.

For more information about Carleton’s involvement, visit the Carnegie Elective Classifications for Sustainability website.

About Carleton College

Consistently ranked among the nation’s top liberal arts institutions, Carleton is a private college of about 2,000 students located in Northfield, Minnesota, just 45 minutes south of the Twin Cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul. Nationally recognized as the nation’s top college for undergraduate teaching, Carleton is known for its academic rigor, intellectual curiosity, and sense of humor. Carleton offers 33 majors and 39 minors in the arts, humanities, natural sciences, mathematics, and social sciences. Learn more about Carleton on the College website.

About the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching

The mission of the Carnegie Foundation is to catalyze transformational change in education so that every student has the opportunity to live a healthy, dignified, and fulfilling life. Enacted by an act of Congress in 1906, the Foundation has a rich history of driving transformational change in the education sector, including the establishment of TIAA-CREF and the creation of the Education Testing Service, the GRE, Pell Grants, and the Carnegie Classifications for Higher Education. 

About the American Council on Education (ACE)

ACE unites and leads higher education institutions toward a shared vision for the future. With more than 1,600 member institutions, ACE drives solutions for today’s challenges, advances public policy, and shapes the higher education sector to serve a diverse student population. Learn more at acenet.edu or follow ACE on X (formerly Twitter) @ACEducation.

json.title: Carleton is one of nation’s first colleges to earn new Carnegie classification for sustainability

Geoffrey Jing joined the consulting firm Bain & Company after he graduated from Carleton College, taking the well-worn path funneling top students into high-paying jobs at leading corporate consulting firms.

He figured that, like many before him, he would work at the firm for two years and then jump to something else.

He figured wrong. Three months into the job, he quit and soon jumped to a start-up called Sieve, which builds data sets and environments for labs developing A.I. models.

“I wanted to spend more of my early career building more closely in A.I.,” Mr. Jing, 23, said.

Read more from The New York Times.
json.excerpt: Jing joined the consulting firm Bain & Company after he graduated from Carleton, but left after 3 months to join a start-up that builds data sets and environments for labs developing AI models.
json.title: Geoffrey Jing ’25 featured in New York Times story on AI start-ups

Four Carleton alumni are traveling to Japan this fall to take part in the Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) program: Alejo Enriquez-Lynd ’26, Zaria Kelly ’25, Alek Pochan ’26, and Lucas Schattenmann ’26.

Established in 1987, JET remains the only teaching exchange program managed by the Japanese government, drawing instructors from over 80 countries worldwide. The program has two pathway options: Assistant Language Teacher (ALT) or Coordinator for International Relations (CIR).

The majority of JET participants — including Enriquez-Lynd, Kelly, and Pochan — have no Japanese fluency requirement and serve as ALTs, teaching English in local schools. CIRs, in contrast, require a high degree of Japanese fluency and are contracted by local government offices to perform a wide range of duties under the umbrella of international relations. Schattenmann, Carleton’s only CIR for this year, will work with translation and interpretation, outreach to foreign residents, education, and exchange activities.

All four of this year’s JET Carls are excited to improve their Japanese language skills and immerse themselves in their respective living locations.

“I’m really excited to be in [Osaka], a big city with lots of things to do and great access to the rest of Japan,” Enriquez-Lynd said. “Osaka is also basically next door to Kyoto, so I’m excited to be able to visit the friends I made over my study abroad there pretty easily… Also, as much as I love Japan and I’m excited to actually live there, I’m really passionate about sharing my own American-Mexican culture with the world, and JET is a really great way to do that.”

“I am looking forward to showing my students different parts of American culture that they had no idea about, and hopefully inspire them to travel here one day!” Kelly added. “My personal goal for this program is also to immerse myself as much as possible into the culture and make an impact on the community I will be living in. It is very important to me that I not only be an observer or consumer of my community, but also a contributor.”

“I want to be a memorable role model for kids and help them feel a sense of achievement,” Pochan said. “I also want to feel truly comfortable living in rural Japan! [I’m excited to] bike around my town, go to bars and talk to older community members, and go to bath houses.”

“I think working alongside Japanese colleagues and living my daily life in the language for a sustained period of time will really accelerate my learning and keep me motivated,” Schattenmann said. “I’m excited about many of the responsibilities I’ll be taking on as a CIR, [like] cultural exchange and translating… I’m already thinking of ideas for events or projects I might be able to help with during my time there. I’m motivated to make my mark and bring positive change to the town I’ll be working in.”

Enriquez-Lynd, Kelly, Pochan, and Schattenmann all have a unique perspective and experiences from Carleton that inspired them to apply for this opportunity.

Enriquez-Lynd, a double major in Japanese language & literature and mathematics, is interested in exploring the intersection of language learning, community building, and pedagogy. He realized his interest in teaching in part through Professor Deanna Haunsperger’s Methods of Teaching Mathematics course at Carleton.

“Obviously Deanna is a great professor who’s incredibly passionate about teaching, and she got me excited about actually doing it, but the course itself was surprisingly relevant to teaching English abroad,” Enriquez-Lynd said. “Similar to English in Japan, math is a subject a lot of students struggle with, and can often be taught in a way that overemphasizes rote memorization without much opportunity for real creativity. Her class inspired me to try to be the teacher I wished I had!”

Kelly, who majored in classical studies, learned how to be open to new experiences and not let fear of failure hold her back at Carleton — she will bring that energy abroad with her.

“Some of my best memories at Carleton were ones where I did something outside of my comfort zone and enjoyed it,” she said. “Carleton also taught me that I am capable of doing difficult things and equipped me with the critical thinking skills, adaptability, and resourcefulness to get through them. Studying abroad in Japan in my sophomore year was my first time overseas, and was the experience that made a major impact on my worldview and shaped the person I am today. I got to see, do, and learn about things that I had never even known had existed. It was truly life changing.”

As a religion major with leadership experience ranging from Ultimate Frisbee team captain to leading a local church youth group, Pochan was focused on why the teaching aspect of JET was right for him and a good fit with his experiences, rather than just his excitement to live in a foreign country — even though both were important in his deliberation around applying.

“It will be great to get some classroom experience,” he added, “because I think I may want to keep teaching high school or middle school in the future.”

Another double major, this time in computer science alongside Japanese language & literature, Schattenmann came to Carleton with “close to zero” Japanese language ability, citing Carleton’s “incredible Japanese education” for his current language skills and the ability to continue learning and adapting, which he knows will be crucial during his time living abroad.

“I think this is a great opportunity for career advancement and Japanese language acquisition, which I think will feel very fulfilling and serve me well into the future,” Schattenmann said. “I’m not quite sure what I’ll do after JET yet, but I figure this is something which will take shape as I continue with the program.”

JET participants can remain in Japan for up to five years, allowing for deep cultural immersion and extension into multiple career paths. 

“I just want to do the best job I possibly can!” Enriquez-Lynd said. “If I can inspire one student to pursue learning English more seriously or travel the world, I’d be immensely proud.”

For any current or future Carls interested in applying for the JET program, each of this year’s participating alumni recommended talking to the Carleton Japanese department — they thanked every professor personally! — and getting in touch with the Office of Student Fellowships, which they all mentioned as extraordinarily helpful in the application process.

But the most important piece of advice they had? Just go for it!

“Ultimately,” Schattenmann said, “as long as you keep up consistent enthusiasm for sharing your culture with others and learning Japanese, you will be just fine.”

json.title: Four Carleton alumni selected for Japan Exchange and Teaching Program

Stephen Mohring, professor of art, has received an inaugural Periclean Faculty Leader (PFL) Course Grant. Funding from this Project Pericles grant will support the development of a new ACE course at Carleton, Habitats and Humanity: Considering Built Spaces, which will be taught for the first time in Spring 2027.

Mohring’s course will consider the built environment — often viewed as a static object — as a dynamic intersection of personal desire, artistic expression, social justice, and structural engineering. Students will bridge the gap between architectural idealism and pragmatic reality, examining how built spaces function as social infrastructure and how theoretical assumptions of modern design and the politics of housing dictate who gets to feel “at home.” A partnership with the local Habitat for Humanity chapter will enable students to engage directly with the Rice County housing landscape, making the economic and sociopolitical realities of habitation tangible, moving students from abstract discussions of spatial planning into applied community action.

Project Pericles’ PFL program supports faculty who are dedicated to incorporating civic and community engagement into the curriculum while empowering students to use their academic knowledge to tackle real-world problems.
json.excerpt: Mohring is professor of art at Carleton.
json.title: Stephen Mohring awarded Periclean Faculty Leader Course Grant

Kiley Kost, lecturer in German, and Seth Peabody, assistant professor of German, co-edited a special issue of the journal German Politics and Society on “Cultures of Climate Action in Germany,” which is available open access. Kost and Peabody also co-authored the issue’s introduction with their co-editors.

In addition, Peabody published an article in the special issue, “Bicycle Greenwishing: Images of Sustainability and Infrastructures of Solidarity in Munich and Berlin,” co-authored with Jennifer Hosek of Queen’s University in Canada.

Carleton announced its adoption of a no-loan financial aid policy on September 14, 2026, which led to news coverage from various local and national news outlets. This coverage included:

  • “Carleton College Adopts No-Loan Financial Aid Policy” from Inside Higher Ed
    • This piece was also included in the “Quick Takes” section of the September 15 edition of the outlet’s email newsletter.
  • “Carleton College drops loans from financial aid, reducing long-term cost for many students” from The Minnesota Star Tribune
  • President Alison Byerly was interviewed live on FOX 9 Minneapolis-St. Paul
    • The segment is available to watch on the FOX 9 YouTube channel.
  • “Carleton College students will be able to graduate debt-free after school eliminates loans” from CBS News Minnesota
    • This story was also distributed by Yahoo News.
  • “Carleton College eliminates loans” from a Minnesota Today segment aired by MPR News
  • “Carleton to Eliminate Loans from Financial Aid Packages Beginning in 2027” from KYMN
  • “Carleton to eliminate loans for new, continuing students” from Northfield News
  • “Carleton College removes loans from financial aid packages” from KTTC and “Carleton College To Eliminate Loans” from KLGR
  • The announcement was included in the Chronicle of Higher Education‘s Daily Briefing newsletter for September 16
  • The announcement was part of MinnPost’s daily news roundup for September 16
  • “Carleton College announces new ‘no loan’ financial aid policy” from Bring Me the News
  • “The number of colleges getting rid of student debt is growing” from Business Insider
  • “Colleges Once Saw High Tuition as a Sign of Quality. Now They’re Slashing Prices” from The Wall Street Journal

This story will be updated as more coverage is published.

json.title: Carleton no-loan financial aid policy covered by local and national news outlets
